name: Cymatics

card.summary: The study of visible patterns that sound and vibration form in sand, liquid or paste, which some wellness communities extend into claims that specific frequencies shape or heal the body.
card.aka: sound visualisation; Chladni figures; frequency healing
card.note: Cymatic patterns are established physics; healing and appearance claims built on them are not tested in human trials.

quick.overview:
Cymatics is the visualisation of vibration: a plate, membrane or liquid is vibrated and powder or water forms geometric patterns along nodal lines. The term was coined by Swiss physician Hans Jenny, building on earlier work by Hooke, Chladni and Faraday [1].

In wellness and fringe circles the patterns are used to support the idea that sound frequencies can organise or repair the body, which some people connect to skin, face and body improvement. The physics is standard classical wave theory; the health applications have no published human trials.
quick.how: People watch or make cymatic patterns for interest, or use sound-frequency tracks and tools they describe as healing. In practice this is listening or exposure to tones rather than any procedure applied to the face or body.
quick.risks: Listening to tones is not a recognised medical treatment, and the main concern raised by clinicians in similar sound-therapy contexts is delay of conventional care. Loud sound exposure can harm hearing.

lead: Cymatics, from the Greek kyma meaning wave, is the study of modal vibrational phenomena in which a plate, diaphragm or membrane is vibrated and regions of maximum and minimum displacement are made visible with particles, paste or liquid. The word was introduced by Swiss physician Hans Jenny (1904-1972).[1]

The roots go back to Robert Hooke's observation in 1680 of patterns in flour on a bowed glass plate, then Ernst Chladni's systematic work in 1787, whose patterns are called Chladni figures, and Michael Faraday's studies of patterns on vibrated liquids, now called Faraday waves.[1][2] Jenny published Kymatik from 1967, using a wider range of frequencies and describing the forms as manifestations of an invisible force field; he was a student of anthroposophist Rudolf Steiner.[1]

In wellness circles, cymatic imagery is cited as support for the view that sound frequencies can shape matter in the body, and so heal or rejuvenate it. This is a community belief layered on top of the physics; Wikipedia states the physics of Chladni figures is best explained by classical physics, with shapes determined by the vibrating body's geometry.[1]

chain: Sound frequency forms ordered patterns in matter
Believers extend this to tissue in the body
angle.text: Some practitioners of frequency healing say specific tones can influence the body and thus skin and general wellbeing. Cymatics itself is the visualisation of vibration patterns, not a cosmetic treatment.

paras: When a plate is driven at a resonant frequency, particles move away from antinodes and collect along nodal lines where vibration is minimal, forming repeatable geometric figures.[1][3] Higher frequencies generally produce more intricate patterns.[3]
Chladni's law relates the vibration frequency of a flat circular plate to the numbers of diametric and radial nodes.[2]
Hooke (1680), Chladni (1787) and Faraday laid the groundwork, and Jenny named and popularised the field in the 1960s with signal generators and diverse media.[1]

Proponents of frequency healing cite cymatic images as evidence that sound organises matter, and extend this to the body. Scientific papers that mention cymatics are mostly about engineering uses, such as flexural-wave cloaking in structured plates and sound during resin curing, or speculative theoretical work on coherent water.[4][5][6]
No studies found. The related research in the literature concerns materials and wave physics, and a review on sound, light and vibration as tools to manage microbes.[4]

timeline.event: Robert Hooke observes nodal patterns in flour on a bowed glass plate.[1]
Hans Jenny publishes Kymatik and coins cymatics.[1]
